title: FeaTok: Feature-Loss Tokenization for Image Generation

paper.title: FeaTok: Feature-Loss Tokenization for Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Discrete image generators learn the distribution of tokens produced by an image tokenizer.
These token representations should be easy for generators to model,
not merely enable faithful image reconstruction.
Yet these tokenizers are commonly trained to reconstruct pixels,
which prioritizes low-level fidelity and may disrupt representation structure
useful for generation.
Motivated by feature-predictive self-supervised learning,
we introduce feature-loss tokenization (FeaTok), which trains discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained features rather than pixels.
Ablations across SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, and DINOv3
show better generative performance with FeaTok. In class-conditional generation, FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto frontier, reducing gFDr6 at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 by up to 29 % 29\% over the strongest discrete baselines and outperforming the strongest unguided continuous baseline (RAEv2) with 38 × 38\times less sampling compute.
FeaTok also achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores than prior art without reward-based training and surpasses continuous and discrete text-conditional baselines on three benchmarks with only 500 500 fine-tuning updates after pre-training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image generation enables machines to create new visual content, supporting applications ranging from creative design to multimodal interaction. A growing body of work represents images as discrete tokens and models them autoregressively ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Discrete tokens share the interface of language models, which makes them a natural choice for unified multimodal models. They also sample an image with an order of magnitude less compute than continuous diffusion models, as shown in Fig. 1 . Image generation quality depends on discrete tokens that are both expressive and easy for a generator to model. Previous discrete tokenizers focus on reconstruction performance, which targets the first property, expressivity . However, generation also depends on the second property, which we call generative learnability : how easily a generator fits the token distribution at a given budget. These two properties do not always align, as observed for both continuous and discrete image tokenizers and generators ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Ramanujan et al., 2025 ) . Generative learnability is related to the structure of a representation ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) , which is in turn induced by the training target. Pixel reconstruction prioritizes high-variance image details over features useful for perception ( Balestriero and Lecun, 2024 ) , and using self-supervised learning (SSL) objectives to predict features instead of pixels yields more semantically meaningful representations ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . We refer to the representations of encoders trained with SSL objectives in feature space as pretrained visual features (see Def. 1 ). Moreover, RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) and RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) show that the benefits of pretrained visual features go beyond representation learning and successfully transfer to image generation. Wang et al. (2024) trained discrete tokens by reconstructing the features of image-understanding encoders instead of pixels, and showed that these tokens can outperform pixel-trained VQ tokens for image generation. Yet the discrete tokenizers that followed still use pixel reconstruction as the central loss, and add pretrained visual features with additional losses ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . This raises the question of whether pixel reconstruction loss is essential for modern discrete tokenizer training used for downstream image generation . We argue that it is not. Feature objectives should shape both the encoder, pretrained in feature space, and the discrete tokens. We introduce feature-loss tokenization ( FeaTok ), which separates discrete representation learning from image reconstruction. Instead of a pixel decoder and a pixel reconstruction loss, a feature decoder that reconstructs pretrained visual features shapes the discrete tokens. A separate image decoder is trained with pixel losses on detached tokens and only renders generated token sequences, so pixel losses never shape the discrete representation. We additionally discretize the encoder’s global representation ( e.g. , CLS token), and generate it before the patch tokens, giving them image-level context. We call this global-augmented generative modelling. Ablations in Sec. 2.2 show that FeaTok has better spatial structure and generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses for all four encoders we study, and that global-augmented modelling contributes to this improvement. On class-conditional ImageNet-1k ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) at × 256 256\!\times\!256 , FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto front for image generation (Fig. 1 ). We measure quality by gFDr6, the mean Fréchet-distance ratio across six feature spaces rather than the Inception space alone ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . FeaTok improves on the strongest discrete baselines by 29 % 29\% without guidance and by 25 % 25\% with it, and outperforms recent continuous generators at a matched sampling cost in both settings. The gains grow at × 512 512\!\times\!512 : relative to the previously best discrete model (BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ), FeaTok reduces gFDr6 by 43 % 43\% without guidance and 39 % 39\% with guidance, up from 32 % 32\% and 25 % 25\% at × 256 256\!\times\!256 , and it also outperforms RAE. FeaTok further achieves higher rewards than discrete and continuous baselines on three human-preference models ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) without reward-based training. Finally, reusing the ImageNet-trained tokenizer, FeaTok surpasses the baselines on three text-to-image benchmarks ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2024 ) after 75 75 K pretraining updates and only 500 500 fine-tuning updates. Discrete tokens shaped by feature losses alone are therefore competitive with continuous representations while sampling at a fraction of the cost, which makes them a practical substrate for unified multimodal models.

sections.heading: 2 Feature-loss tokenization
sections.text: In this section, we present FeaTok , which learns discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained visual features. We use this term to distinguish representations by their pretraining objective. Definition 1 . We define pretrained visual features as representations of encoders learned by self-supervision in feature space, including language–image contrastive learning ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) and self-distillation ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Siméoni et al., 2026 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . Encoders trained by pixel reconstruction ( He et al., 2022 ) are excluded. We next describe how FeaTok uses these features to train the tokenizer with feature losses (Fig. 2 ).

sections.heading: 2.1 Learning discrete tokens with feature loss only
sections.text: Conventional discrete tokenizers ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ; Jia et al., 2025 ; Bachmann et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ; Yu et al., 2026 ) consist of an encoder E E , a quantizer Q Q , and a pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} . Given an image x x partitioned into N N patches, the encoder E E produces N N feature vectors, one per patch, which the quantizer Q Q maps to discrete tokens z 1 : N = Q ( E ( x ) ) z_{1:N}=Q(E(x)) . The pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} then reconstructs the image as x ^ = D pix ( z 1 : N ) \hat{x}=D_{\rm pix}(z_{1:N}) . Tokenizers are typically trained as an autoencoder with a pixel-level objective ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm pix} that combines pixel reconstruction losses ( ℓ 1 \ell_{1} , ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ), perceptual losses (LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , GRAM ( Lu et al., 2026a ) ), and adversarial losses ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) . Once the tokenizer is trained, an autoregressive model conditioned on class labels or text prompts c c learns the distribution p ϕ ( z 1 : N ∣ c ) p_{\phi}(z_{1:N}\mid c) of the resulting token sequences using the cross-entropy loss. Shaping discrete tokens with feature losses. FeaTok follows the autoencoder-style tokenizer design, but learns the discrete tokens by reconstructing features rather than pixels (see Fig. 2 ). Concretely, we add a feature decoder D feat D_{\rm feat} that maps the discrete tokens z 1 : N z_{1:N} to a prediction y ^ 1 : N = D feat ( z 1 : N ) \hat{y}_{1:N}=D_{\rm feat}(z_{1:N}) of a feature target y 1 : N y_{1:N} . We train the encoder, quantizer, and feature decoder to match this prediction to the target using a loss ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm feat} that combines ℓ 1 \ell_{1} , ℓ 2 \ell_{2} , and cosine distances. For the feature target, following the insights in Singh et al. (2026) , we use an average of features from multiple layers of the frozen vision encoder E ^ \hat{E} , y 1 : N ( x ) = | 𝒦 | − 1 ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 LN k ( E ^ ( k ) ( x ) 1 : N ) y_{1:N}(x)=|\mathcal{K}|^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\operatorname{LN}_{k}(\hat{E}^{(k)}(x)_{1:N}) , where 𝒦 \mathcal{K} contains four evenly spaced encoder layers and LayerNorm ( Ba et al., 2016 ) normalizes each layer’s features before averaging. This target is intended to combine visual detail from earlier layers with semantic information from later layers, balancing expressivity and generative learnability. While we retain the pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} and its pixel-level loss ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm{pix}} during training, we stop the gradients at the decoder input. This preserves the ability to decode tokens back into images while preventing the pixel reconstruction losses from shaping the token distribution. Figure 2: FeaTok tokenizer and generation pipeline. Blue denotes the conventional discrete tokenizer and orange our contributions. Only feature losses shape the discrete tokens: ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm feat} trains D feat D_{\rm feat} to reconstruct the multi-layer target y y of the frozen encoder E ^ \hat{E} from both global and patch tokens, while ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm pix} trains only D pix D_{\rm pix} on detached patch tokens. The generator (not shown) models the global token from Q global Q_{\rm global} together with the patch tokens from Q patch Q_{\rm patch} . Leveraging global tokens. In addition to patch features, various vision encoders supply a global representation, e.g. , a CLS token in DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Siméoni et al., 2026 ) or a global pooling token in SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . Replacing pixel reconstruction with feature reconstruction losses naturally suggests discretizing this global feature along with patches. The benefit of doing so is that it allows us to define a hierarchical generative model that first generates the global token and then the patch tokens conditioned on it which simplifies the conditional distributions of the patch tokens by providing a global context. This global representation is generally ignored by discrete tokenizers trained using pixel-reconstruction losses, as the pixel reconstruction over patches does not provide direct supervision on the global feature discretization. Prior work follows a similar global-to-local strategy, using learned holistic tokens ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) , coarse-to-fine token sequences ( Bachmann et al., 2025 ) , or separately generated semantic codes ( Lavoie et al., 2025 ) . In our case, the global token directly discretizes the pretrained encoder’s global representation. Specifically, we use separate quantizers, Q global Q_{\rm global} and Q patch Q_{\rm patch} , for global and patch features, respectively. The feature decoder D feat D_{\rm feat} takes both global and patch tokens and reconstructs the combined target y = ( y global , y 1 : N ) y=(y_{\rm global},y_{1:N}) using the feature loss ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm{feat}} . This yields a discrete global token z global z_{\rm global} , which we model jointly with the patch tokens using the following factorization: p ϕ ( z global , z 1 : N ∣ c ) = p ϕ ( z global ∣ c ) ∏ i = 1 N p ϕ ( z i ∣ z global , z < i , c ) . p_{\phi}(z_{\rm global},z_{1:N}\mid c)=p_{\phi}(z_{\rm global}\mid c)\,\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{\phi}(z_{i}\mid z_{\rm global},z_{<i},c). (1) where c c denotes the class label or text prompt. During inference, the generator first samples the global token and then samples patch tokens conditioned on both global and external conditions. Combined training objective. We train the tokenizer and pixel decoder jointly using the feature and pixel losses described above. Following prior work on semantic preservation during tokenizer training ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Du et al., 2026 ) , we also include an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularizer ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\rm reg} between the last-layer features h h and h ^ \hat{h} of the trainable and frozen encoders. The weights λ reg \lambda_{\rm reg} and λ pix \lambda_{\rm pix} balance the loss terms, and sg \mathrm{sg} stops gradients at the pixel decoder input. Once the tokenizer is trained, we keep it fixed and train an autoregressive generator on its tokens using teacher forcing. We combine the cross-entropy loss for the global token with the average loss over patch tokens, weighted by λ global \lambda_{\rm global} and λ patch \lambda_{\rm patch} , respectively. These weights control the emphasis on global and patch prediction independently of the number of patches.

Details of ablation setups are given in App. C . Feature targets work better than pixel-only or mixed feature–pixel targets. Feature supervision improves the generation over pixel supervision for three of the four encoders, as shown in Fig. 3 . With patch-only generation, replacing pixel targets with feature targets lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, while combining pixel and feature losses, i.e. , letting gradients from both decoders update the discrete tokens, gives intermediate results. The feature target raises this dependence and lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, showing that the feature target improves the token structure for generation. SigLIP2 is the exception, possibly because, unlike the other three encoders, it is not trained only in feature space. Its training adds a text decoder that generates captions of whole images and of specific regions ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . With the global token, FeaTok with SigLIP2 overtakes the counterpart trained with pixel reconstruction losses. Leveraging features from multiple layers improves generation. The four-layer average gives the best measured gFID for each encoder in Fig. 4 , with global-augmented generation throughout. Compared with the first and last layers, respectively, averaging yields the best generation performance consistently across all encoders. sections.heading: 3.1 ImageNet-1k generation at × 256 256\!\times\!256
sections.text: We train our × 256 256\!\times\!256 FeaTok tokenizers on ImageNet-1k using SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , and DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) encoders, with a vocabulary size of 65,536 65,536 . For each tokenizer, we train the same autoregressive generator as BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , the previous state-of-the-art discrete model for ImageNet-1k, with our global-augmented modelling. App. A specifies the implementation details including vision encoder versions, tokenizer and generator instantiations, etc. Fréchet distance in the Inception space can misrank modern generative models, and measuring it in stronger feature spaces such as DINOv2 agrees better with human judgments ( Stein et al., 2023 ) . We therefore report gFDr6, the mean Fréchet-distance ratio across Inception-v3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) , ConvNeXt V2 ( Woo et al., 2023 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) , SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , and CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) feature spaces, following Yang et al. (2026) . In App. E we detail the sampling configurations for each model. In App. F we report gFID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and precision, recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) , density and coverage ( Naeem et al., 2020 ) in Inception space as complementary diagnostics. Unless stated otherwise, baselines are evaluated by us using their released setups. FeaTok outperforms discrete models. In Tab. 1 we compare FeaTok using different vision encoders and two model sizes to existing discrete image generative models in terms of gFDr6 and its per-feature metrics. All four FeaTok-L variants outperform the strongest prior discrete baseline in gFDr6, showing consistent gains across four pretrained visual feature encoders satisfying Def. 1 . FeaTok-DINOv3 is the strongest discrete model at both generator scales, with and without guidance. The largest improvements appear without guidance, where we reduce the prior baseline gFDr6 of 4.38 4.38 from VFMTok2-XXL ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) to 3.13 3.13 . With guidance, we reduce the 4.11 4.11 gFDr6 of BAR-L to 3.08 3.08 . Increasing the generator from base to large consistently improves gFDr6; for DINOv3, it decreases from 3.58 3.58 to 3.13 3.13 without guidance and from 3.39 3.39 to 3.08 3.08 with guidance. Importantly, these generation gains do not coincide with improved reconstruction: rFID remains nearly constant across FeaTok tokenizers ( 0.92 0.92 – 1.01 1.01 ; App. C.3 ), reinforcing that reconstruction fidelity alone does not explain generative performance. sections.heading: 3.3 Extension to text-to-image generation
sections.text: Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of FeaTok by applying it to text-to-image (T2I) generation. Following RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) , we use BLIP-3o datasets ( Chen et al., 2025 ) (Long-Caption, Short-Caption, and JourneyDB) for pre-training and BLIP-3o-60K for fine-tuning. We replace the class conditioning in FeaTok with a sequence of text embeddings provided by Qwen3-0.6B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) to enable T2I generation, re-using our FeaTok-SigLIP2 tokenizer trained on ImageNet-1k. We pre-train 75k updates with batch size 2048 2048 , while baselines use 150k updates with batch size 1024 1024 , giving the same total number of training examples processed. Then we further fine-tune the pre-trained model for 500 500 updates, while baselines are fine-tuned for approximately 3k updates. After pre-training, FeaTok is broadly comparable to RAEv2. It is slightly lower on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) ( 0.611 0.611 versus 0.624 0.624 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) ( 79.8 79.8 versus 81.7 81.7 ), but higher on GenAI-Bench ( Li et al., 2024a ) ( 0.668 0.668 versus 0.638 0.638 ). After only 500 500 additional updates, FeaTok exceeds RAEv2 on all three benchmarks: 0.837 0.837 versus 0.827 0.827 on GenEval, 0.698 0.698 versus 0.680 0.680 on GenAI-Bench, and 83.4 83.4 versus 82.3 82.3 on DPG-Bench. The comparison with BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) isolates the effect of the tokenizer directly, whose tokenizer is trained with pixel losses and a feature-alignment loss using SigLIP2. After pre-training, FeaTok is ahead of BAR on GenEval, slightly ahead on GenAI-Bench, and tied on DPG-Bench. After fine-tuning, all three benchmarks rank FeaTok above BAR, with 0.837 0.837 versus 0.817 0.817 on GenEval, 0.698 0.698 versus 0.688 0.688 on GenAI-Bench, and 83.4 83.4 versus 81.7 81.7 on DPG-Bench. The advantage of feature-loss tokens over mixed tokens thus carries over from class-conditional to text-to-image generation. We provide several T2I qualitative examples in Fig. 6 . sections.heading: 4 Related work
sections.text: Pretrained representations for continuous generation. Continuous generators show that the pretraining objective of the features matters. RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) and RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) train diffusion models in the feature spaces of pretrained vision encoders, paired with learned image decoders, and RAE finds that MAE features ( He et al., 2022 ) reconstruct best but generate worse than DINOv2 features. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025b ) aligns intermediate SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ) features with pretrained representations, where MAE is the weakest of the tested targets, and DDT ( Wang et al., 2026 ) adopts this alignment. REG ( Wu et al., 2025 ) denoises a pretrained class token together with the image latents, VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns VAE latents with a pretrained vision encoder, and REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025 ) tunes the VAE and the diffusion model end to end with the REPA loss. Discrete tokenization with pretrained representations. VQ-VAE ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ) learns discrete image tokens through pixel reconstruction, and later tokenizers simplify the quantizer ( Yu et al., 2024a ; Mentzer et al., 2024 ) . Wang et al. (2024) train tokenizers to reconstruct the features from image understanding encoders, and in autoregressive generation all but the MAE teacher outperform pixel-trained VQGAN tokens. Recent tokenizers keep pixel reconstruction as the central objective and add pretrained encoder features through feature alignment ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , semantic regularization ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) , self-distillation ( Du et al., 2026 ) , or feature reconstruction from several encoder depths ( Jia et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) . TA-Tok ( Han et al., 2025 ) trains feature-reconstructed tokens for unified multimodal models, but decodes images through pixel-trained VQ tokens or latents. In FeaTok, only pretrained visual features (Def. 1 ) shape the tokens, which reconstruct a multi-layer target and include a quantized global token.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented FeaTok, a discrete image tokenizer whose tokens are shaped only by feature reconstruction, while a pixel decoder trained on detached tokens renders them into images. We also discretize the encoder’s global representation and model it together with the patch tokens. Across four pretrained encoders, FeaTok generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses. FeaTok achieves the best gFDr6 among the evaluated discrete generators on ImageNet at × 256 256\!\times\!256 and × 512 512\!\times\!512 , outperforms continuous generators at a matched sampling cost, achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores, and transfers to text-to-image generation after pretraining and only 500 500 fine-tuning updates. We believe these results are a step toward effective discrete representations for unified multimodal modeling, and that the low sampling cost of FeaTok makes it attractive for scaling multimodal training.

We follow BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , the previous state-of-the-art method, in our tokenizer and generator training. BAR uses bit representations for its tokens and an autoregressive model with a masked modeling head to predict the bits within each token. Ablation protocols and variants are described in App. C . Note that DINOv2-L uses a patch size of 14 14 , whereas the other encoders use a patch size of 16 16 . sections.heading: Appendix B Generator implementation details
sections.text: We follow BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) to implement the generative model, with our global-augmented generative modelling. BAR generative model. Recall that BAR learns tokens with FSQ in a bit representation and models their distribution with an adapted autoregressive model. Instead of a single categorical prediction over the entire codebook, BAR uses a lightweight masked bit modeling head. During training, some bits of the target token are masked, and the head learns to recover them with a bit-wise cross-entropy objective. During sampling, it starts with all bits masked and progressively fills them in, conditioning later predictions on the bits already revealed. The autoregressive context stays fixed during these within-token steps. Once the token is complete, it becomes part of the context for the next token. This avoids an output distribution with one logit per codebook entry while allowing dependencies among a token’s bits. The token-level training objective described in Sec. 2.1 is ℒ gen = 𝔼 ( z , c ) ​ [ λ global ​ ℓ CE ​ ( z global ∣ c ) + λ patch ​ 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℓ CE ​ ( z i ∣ z global , z < i , c ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\rm gen}=\mathbb{E}_{(z,c)}\!\left[\lambda_{\rm global}\,\ell_{\rm CE}(z_{\rm global}\mid c)+\lambda_{\rm patch}\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{\rm CE}(z_{i}\mid z_{\rm global},z_{<i},c)\right], (4) where ℓ CE \ell_{\rm CE} is the conditional cross-entropy prediction loss. Our implementation. We instantiate the conditional cross-entropy in Eq. 4 with BAR’s masked bit modeling objective ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Let B j = ( B j ​ 1 , … , B j ​ d ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } d B_{j}=(B_{j1},\ldots,B_{jd})\in\{0,1\}^{d} be the clean bit representation of token z j z_{j} , with d = 16 d=16 , where ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , d } \ell\in\{1,\ldots,d\} indexes the bits. For each token, we sample a masking ratio r j r_{j} and mask n j = round ⁡ ( d ​ r j ) n_{j}=\mathrm{round}(d\,r_{j}) of its bits, chosen uniformly at random, giving a mask m j ∈ { 0 , 1 } d m_{j}\in\{0,1\}^{d} with m j ​ ℓ = 1 m_{j\ell}=1 if bit ℓ \ell is masked. Following BAR, patch tokens draw r j = max ⁡ ( 1 − t , 1 / d ) r_{j}=\max(1-t,\,1/d) with t = σ ⁡ ( ϵ ) t=\sigma(\epsilon) , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.8 2 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.8^{2}) , and σ \sigma the sigmoid. The global token, which BAR does not have, draws t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] instead. The lower bound r j ≥ 1 / d r_{j}\geq 1/d ensures n j ≥ 1 n_{j}\geq 1 , so every token has at least one masked bit to predict. Replacing each masked bit B j ​ ℓ B_{j\ell} by a mask symbol gives B ~ j \widetilde{B}_{j} . The prediction head estimates the likelihood of the clean bits conditioned on B ~ j \widetilde{B}_{j} , the masking ratio r j r_{j} , and the autoregressive context C j C_{j} . The mask positions are already encoded by the mask symbols in B ~ j \widetilde{B}_{j} . During teacher forcing, C global = c C_{\rm global}=c and C i = ( z global , z < i , c ) C_{i}=(z_{\rm global},z_{<i},c) for patch i i . Let 𝒮 \mathcal{S} be a set of token positions, either the global token 𝒮 global = { global } \mathcal{S}_{\rm global}=\{\mathrm{global}\} or the patch tokens 𝒮 patch = { 1 , … , N } \mathcal{S}_{\rm patch}=\{1,\ldots,N\} . Each term − log p ϕ , ℓ ( B j ​ ℓ ∣ ⋅ ) -\log p_{\phi,\ell}(B_{j\ell}\mid\cdot) is the cross-entropy between the observed bit and the head’s two-class prediction, so Eq. 6 specifies the token prediction loss ℓ CE \ell_{\rm CE} in Eq. 4 for our masked bit modeling head. Because the normalization pools the bits of all tokens in 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , a token with more masked bits contributes more, so the patch loss is a bit-weighted average over patch positions rather than exactly the uniform average 1 N ∑ i = 1 N \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} of Eq. 4 . The bit prediction task additionally conditions on the visible bits within the current token, making it a denoising cross-entropy objective rather than an exact evaluation of the complete token’s autoregressive negative log-likelihood. FeaTok retains the BAR generator backbone and masked-bit prediction mechanism while changing the tokenizer that supplies its training codes. For global-augmented generation, we additionally prepend a sampled global token to the patch token sequence. This global token is image-dependent and thus distinct from the external class label or text condition c c . BAR-B and BAR-L denote the base and large generator configurations. In our experiments for ImageNet-1k at 256 × 256 256\times 256 , each patch token contains 16 16 bits, corresponding to 2 16 2^{16} possible tokens. For ImageNet-1k at 512 × 512 512\times 512 , we use 10 10 bits per token following BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . We use allocation to specify the unmasking process for each token during the sampling, e.g. , [ 4 , 4 , 4 , 4 ] [4,4,4,4] specifies four within-token sampling steps, each revealing four bits. These within token sampling steps are distinct from the autoregressive steps over patch positions. The class label enters as repeated condition tokens, and for global-augmented generation the global token is likewise repeated after them. For classifier-free guidance, a fixed fraction of training samples drop their conditions. Most of these drop both the class label and the global token, and the rest drop only one of them, so the generator also learns each condition on its own. sections.heading: C.1 Ablation protocol and sampling without guidance
sections.text: The controlled ablations in Sec. 2.2 compare tokenizer design choices using BAR generators ( Yu et al., 2026 ) specified in App. B at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. We evaluate 50 50 K generated images under a fixed sampling configuration, rather than choosing a separate best sampling configuration for each ablation. We use guidance scale 1.0 1.0 , i.e. , no guidance, sampling temperature 2.0 2.0 , and bit-group allocation [ 4 , 4 , 4 , 4 ] [4,4,4,4] . For more details about the sampling hyperparameters, check App. E . For global-augmented models, the global token is sampled first with the same sampling hyperparameters, and then conditions patch generation. Patch-only models omit the global token, but retain class conditioning. We use the unguided protocol for ablation because it avoids the additional unconditional prediction used for classifier-free guidance and removes guidance strength as an additional sampling hyperparameter. The full results presented in Sec. 2.2 are detailed in Tab. 11 .

sections.heading: C.2 Tokenizers from an MAE encoder
sections.text: We also trained tokenizers from MAE-L/16 ( He et al., 2022 ) , whose features are learned by pixel reconstruction and therefore fall outside Def. 1 . These runs use the same tokenizer and BAR-B generator recipes, with 250 250 K generator steps and 50 50 K samples without guidance at patch temperature 2.0 2.0 and allocation [ 4 , 4 , 4 , 4 ] [4,4,4,4] . They differ in three respects: they omit source-preservation regularization, use the last MAE layer as the feature target, and use MAE’s auxiliary class token as the global token, sampled at temperature 2.5 2.5 and allocation [ 2 , 2 , 5 , 7 ] [2,2,5,7] . MAE-based tokenizers generate poorly under every supervision. With patch-only generation, gFID is 5.74 5.74 for the pixel target, 5.94 5.94 for combined pixel and feature targets, and 6.40 6.40 for the feature target, and global-augmented generation reaches 5.55 5.55 and 5.75 5.75 with the combined and feature targets. Feature supervision thus does not improve MAE-based tokens, and every MAE configuration stays far above the gFID range of Tab. 11 , so we do not pursue MAE further.

sections.heading: C.3 Reconstruction results
sections.text: Tab. 12 reports reconstruction for four source encoders under pixel and feature supervision, using regularized tokenizers throughout. With pixel supervision, the pixel loss trains the encoder and quantizer. With feature supervision, the pixel gradient is cut at the discrete representation, and the feature decoder reconstructs the four-layer-average target. Across the four encoders, rFID ranges from 0.72 0.72 to 1.40 1.40 . The six-space view complements rFID: feature targets improve rFDr6 over pixel targets for SigLIP ( 2.68 2.68 to 2.45 2.45 ), SigLIP2 ( 2.09 2.09 to 2.04 2.04 ), and DINOv3 ( 2.24 2.24 to 2.08 2.08 ), but not DINOv2 ( 1.82 1.82 to 2.06 2.06 ). These reconstruction scores alone do not explain the generation differences in Sec. 3.1 . Pixel fidelity versus perceptual quality. Feature supervision lowers PSNR and SSIM for all four encoders, e.g. , from 20.61 20.61 to 17.45 17.45 PSNR for DINOv3, so the tokens no longer reproduce each input pixel by pixel. For image generation, however, the goal is images that look real to humans, not pixel-exact copies of a given input. PSNR and SSIM compare each reconstruction with its input pixel by pixel, so they penalize small shifts of texture and detail that humans barely notice, and they correlate poorly with human perceptual judgments ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . Distribution-level metrics instead ask whether the images look like real images, and they favor feature supervision. Feature targets improve rFDr6 for three of the four encoders, and the same feature-supervised tokenizers give lower gFID in the controlled ablations (Tab. 11 ), the best gFDr6 among discrete generators (Tab. 1 ), and higher human-preference reward-model scores (Fig. 5 ). The lower paired pixel fidelity is therefore a trade-off rather than a free improvement. Feature-supervised tokens discard some input detail, and not all of it need be perceptually irrelevant, but for generation the trade-off favors feature supervision in the distribution-level and reward-model evaluations above. sections.heading: C.4 Token Structure Measurement
sections.text: Figure 7: Linear separability and generation. Discrete-token probe accuracy on 25 25 K test images versus patch-only gFID on 50 50 K samples without guidance. The gFID axis is log-scaled. Spatial-dependence diagnostic. The spatial dependence in Fig. 3 measures how informative one patch token is about an adjacent patch token in the same image. Rather than estimating MI between complete categorical token IDs, we use a component-wise proxy based on the tokenizer’s binary code representation. Each patch token is represented by 16 16 bits. For each pair of patch positions at a given offset, we estimate the MI, in bits, between pairs of these bits from their joint occurrence frequencies across 25 25 K class-balanced ImageNet training images. We average these estimates over the 256 256 bit pairs, over all position pairs of the offset, and over the four cardinal directions. Higher values indicate stronger statistical dependence between the bits of spatially separated tokens. The same estimator is applied to all eight tokenizers. Each point in Fig. 3 pairs the estimate for adjacent patches with the gFID of the patch-only generator from Tab. 11 . Replacing the pixel target by the feature target raises the dependence for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, but it lowers the dependence for SigLIP2. This diagnostic measures component-wise dependence in the tokenizer’s code parameterization, not MI between full token IDs or the prediction loss of a learned generator. Discrete-token linear probes. We fit linear classifiers on mean-pooled patch bits using 100 100 K training images, select the learning rate and weight decay on 10 10 K validation images, and evaluate on 25 25 K test images held out from probe fitting, averaging accuracy over three training seeds. As in Fig. 3 , Fig. 7 pairs each tokenizer with the gFID of its patch-only generator from Tab. 11 . Replacing the pixel target by the feature target lowers probe accuracy but improves gFID for SigLIP and DINOv2. For SigLIP2, probe accuracy and gFID both worsen, and for DINOv3, both improve. Thus, this measure of linear separability does not consistently track class-conditional generation quality, unlike the spatial dependence in Fig. 3 .

sections.text: This section collects the experimental setup and measurement conventions used in Sec. 3 . Experimental setup. We evaluate class-conditioned image generation on ImageNet-1k ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and 512 × 512 512\times 512 , and text-conditioned generation on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , GenAI-Bench ( Li et al., 2024a ) , and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Reconstruction and generation metrics. For a fixed feature extractor, Fréchet distance compares the empirical means and covariances of real and reconstructed or generated image features. rFID is the tokenizer’s reconstruction measurement that compares the reconstructed images and original images in the Inception space using the ImageNet-1k validation set. gFID compares generated images with the original training images using Fréchet distance in Inception space. We re-use the released reference statistics from Li and He (2026) . We also report gFDr6 introduced by Yang et al. (2026) , which reports generative Fréchet distance in six different feature spaces. The six-space evaluation uses Inception-v3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) , ConvNeXt V2 ( Woo et al., 2023 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) , SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , and CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , with the checkpoints of Yang et al. sections.heading: Appendix F Comparison using conventional gFID and PRDC metrics.
sections.text: In the main paper, we report results in gFDr6 ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . We compare our method with baselines using gFID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and Precision, Recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) , Density, and Coverage ( Naeem et al., 2020 ) in Tab. 14 . Per conventions, we use different hyperparameters during sampling for gFID evaluation than gFDr6. gFID measures the Fréchet distance in the feature space of an Inception-v3 network ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) trained for ImageNet classification. Its sensitivity to ImageNet class information means that it can be lowered substantially without improving the images ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2023 ) , and Inception features represent the content of modern generators poorly, so gFID often disagrees with human raters ( Stein et al., 2023 ; Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) . These problems are most severe at the low values reached by current ImageNet generators. ImageNet validation images score a gFID of 1.68 1.68 against the training set ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , so generators below 2.0 2.0 , and especially below 1.68 1.68 , appear as close to the training data as real images, although their samples remain clearly distinguishable from real ones ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . In this regime, gFID can also be optimized directly: post-training a generator on Inception features lowers its gFID from 3.31 3.31 to 0.81 0.81 without producing the best samples, whereas post-training on modern representations improves object structure while gFID becomes worse ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . gFDr6 addresses these issues by averaging Fréchet distances over six representation spaces, each normalized by the distance between the training and validation sets, so no single feature space dominates and a value of 1 1 means as close to the training data as real validation images. Tab. 14 provides additional evidence. At these low-gFID operating points, improvements in Inception Fréchet distance do not consistently agree with the fidelity diagnostics. Across the ten BAR and FeaTok models, the guided configuration has lower gFID and higher recall in every case, but lower precision in seven and lower density in nine. For example, BAR-B’s gFID improves from 1.64 1.64 to 1.13 1.13 , while precision falls from 0.800 0.800 to 0.775 0.775 and density from 1.153 1.153 to 1.060 1.060 . Recall rises from 0.614 0.614 to 0.660 0.660 . Thus, rather than demonstrating a uniform fidelity gain, these selected configurations often show a fidelity–recall trade-off in the opposite direction to the usual motivation for guidance. Coverage remains near saturation ( 0.994 0.994 – 0.997 0.997 ). The results caution against interpreting a small gFID improvement as an unambiguous improvement in generation quality, motivating evaluation across multiple representations and complementary reward measures. Without guidance, every FeaTok-B model has a lower gFID than BAR-B ( 1.34 1.34 – 1.61 1.61 against 1.64 1.64 ), three of the four FeaTok-L models improve on BAR-L ( 1.15 1.15 – 1.33 1.33 against 1.36 1.36 , with FeaTok-L-SigLIP at 1.37 1.37 ), and FeaTok-L-DINOv3 reaches 1.15 1.15 against 1.61 1.61 for RAEv2. With guidance, three of the four FeaTok-B models improve over BAR-B, while BAR-L reaches the lowest large-model gFID, 1.02 1.02 , against 1.04 1.04 for RAEv2 and 1.05 1.05 for FeaTok-L-DINOv3. These guided values are all well below the 1.68 1.68 of real validation images, in the regime where gFID no longer tracks sample quality. Under gFDr6, which accounts for all six representation spaces, FeaTok-L-DINOv3 improves over BAR-L by 25 % 25\% with guidance (Tab. 1 ). The baselines in Tab. 1 use their released sampling settings, which were selected for gFID, whereas the FeaTok settings there are selected for gFDr6. Tab. 15 therefore also reports gFDr6 for every FeaTok model at its gFID-selected configuration, the one used in Tab. 14 , so that both sides follow the same selection criterion. Under this criterion, all four FeaTok-B models and three of the four FeaTok-L models still improve on the original-decoder BAR model of the same size, with and without guidance. FeaTok-L-DINOv3 reduces gFDr6 from 4.57 4.57 to 3.35 3.35 without guidance and from 4.11 4.11 to 3.45 3.45 with guidance, while FeaTok-L-SigLIP is the exception, at 4.75 4.75 and 4.42 4.42 . sections.heading: Appendix G Sampling-cost measurement
sections.text: TFLOPs. TFLOPs is arithmetic per image, counted with torch.utils.flop_counter in the 2 × 2\times MAC convention, and is therefore hardware-independent unlike wall-clock throughput. It covers the full sampling loop of the generator plus one decoder pass that maps the generated tokens or latents to pixels. Classifier-free guidance duplicates the generator batch and roughly doubles its cost (BAR, FeaTok, SiT, LightningDiT, DDT and the discrete baselines), whereas REPA-E and REG gate the doubled forward to a guidance interval and pay 1.8 × 1.8\times , RAEv2’s internal guidance reuses a single forward and costs nothing, and RAE’s autoguidance adds a smaller second network for + 30 % +30\% . Guidance never duplicates the decoder, since only the conditional sample is decoded. Each decoder is built from its official release and driven through the released sampler’s decode call. Decoder costs range from 0.16 0.16 TFLOPs for the pixel decoder shared by BAR and FeaTok to 0.62 0.62 for the SD-VAE decoder of the latent diffusion baselines. They are small relative to multi-step continuous generators, but not negligible for the cheapest samplers: the pixel decoder adds 15 15 – 32 % 32\% to the generator cost of BAR and FeaTok, and the SD-VAE decoder exceeds the generator cost of the latent one-step models. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22060v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026 FeaTok: Feature-Loss Tokenization for Image Generation Zhang Xiaofeng Affiliation: Mila - Québec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Samuel Lavoie Affiliation: Mila - Québec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Equal contribution Nicolas Beltran-Velez Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: Columbia University Equal contribution Jianhao Yuan Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: University of Oxford Felix Friedrich Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Jakob Verbeek Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Aaron Courville Affiliation: Mila - Québec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: Canada CIFAR AI chair Co-senior authors Michal Drozdzal Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Co-senior authors Adriana Romero-Soriano Affiliation: Mila - Québec AI Institute Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: McGill University Affiliation: Canada CIFAR AI chair Co-senior authors Abstract Discrete image generators learn the distribution of tokens produced by an image tokenizer. These token representations should be easy for generators to model, not merely enable faithful image reconstruction. Yet these tokenizers are commonly trained to reconstruct pixels, which prioritizes low-level fidelity and may disrupt representation structure useful for generation. Motivated by feature-predictive self-supervised learning, we introduce feature-loss tokenization (FeaTok), which trains discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained features rather than pixels. Ablations across SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, and DINOv3 show better generative performance with FeaTok. In class-conditional generation, FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto frontier, reducing gFDr6 at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 by up to 29 % 29\% over the strongest discrete baselines and outperforming the strongest unguided continuous baseline (RAEv2) with 38 × 38\times less sampling compute. FeaTok also achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores than prior art without reward-based training and surpasses continuous and discrete text-conditional baselines on three benchmarks with only 500 500 fine-tuning updates after pre-training. † † Website: https://featok.github.io/ † † correspondence: xiaofeng.zhang@mila.quebec Figure 1: Feature-based discrete tokens enable strong generation. FeaTok models advance the quality–compute Pareto frontier for image generation. We categorize generative image models by how pretrained feature-predictive self-supervised learning representations (Def. 1 ) shape the generated representation or the generator: not at all (pixel-based), together with pixel objectives (mixed), or alone (feature-based). Generation performance on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , where all models sample without guidance. Both axes are log-scaled. 1 Introduction Image generation enables machines to create new visual content, supporting applications ranging from creative design to multimodal interaction. A growing body of work represents images as discrete tokens and models them autoregressively ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Discrete tokens share the interface of language models, which makes them a natural choice for unified multimodal models. They also sample an image with an order of magnitude less compute than continuous diffusion models, as shown in Fig. 1 . Image generation quality depends on discrete tokens that are both expressive and easy for a generator to model. Previous discrete tokenizers focus on reconstruction performance, which targets the first property, expressivity . However, generation also depends on the second property, which we call generative learnability : how easily a generator fits the token distribution at a given budget. These two properties do not always align, as observed for both continuous and discrete image tokenizers and generators ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Ramanujan et al., 2025 ) . Generative learnability is related to the structure of a representation ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) , which is in turn induced by the training target. Pixel reconstruction prioritizes high-variance image details over features useful for perception ( Balestriero and Lecun, 2024 ) , and using self-supervised learning (SSL) objectives to predict features instead of pixels yields more semantically meaningful representations ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . We refer to the representations of encoders trained with SSL objectives in feature space as pretrained visual features (see Def. 1 ). Moreover, RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) and RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) show that the benefits of pretrained visual features go beyond representation learning and successfully transfer to image generation. Wang et al. (2024) trained discrete tokens by reconstructing the features of image-understanding encoders instead of pixels, and showed that these tokens can outperform pixel-trained VQ tokens for image generation. Yet the discrete tokenizers that followed still use pixel reconstruction as the central loss, and add pretrained visual features with additional losses ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . This raises the question of whether pixel reconstruction loss is essential for modern discrete tokenizer training used for downstream image generation . We argue that it is not. Feature objectives should shape both the encoder, pretrained in feature space, and the discrete tokens. We introduce feature-loss tokenization ( FeaTok ), which separates discrete representation learning from image reconstruction. Instead of a pixel decoder and a pixel reconstruction loss, a feature decoder that reconstructs pretrained visual features shapes the discrete tokens. A separate image decoder is trained with pixel losses on detached tokens and only renders generated token sequences, so pixel losses never shape the discrete representation. We additionally discretize the encoder’s global representation ( e.g. , CLS token), and generate it before the patch tokens, giving them image-level context. We call this global-augmented generative modelling. Ablations in Sec. 2.2 show that FeaTok has better spatial structure and generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses for all four encoders we study, and that global-augmented modelling contributes to this improvement. On class-conditional ImageNet-1k ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) at × 256 256\!\times\!256 , FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto front for image generation (Fig. 1 ). We measure quality by gFDr6, the mean Fréchet-distance ratio across six feature spaces rather than the Inception space alone ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . FeaTok improves on the strongest discrete baselines by 29 % 29\% without guidance and by 25 % 25\% with it, and outperforms recent continuous generators at a matched sampling cost in both settings. The gains grow at × 512 512\!\times\!512 : relative to the previously best discrete model (BAR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ), FeaTok reduces gFDr6 by 43 % 43\% without guidance and 39 % 39\% with guidance, up from 32 % 32\% and 25 % 25\% at × 256 256\!\times\!256 , and it also outperforms RAE. FeaTok further achieves higher rewards than discrete and continuous baselines on three human-preference models ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) without reward-based training. Finally, reusing the ImageNet-trained tokenizer, FeaTok surpasses the baselines on three text-to-image benchmarks ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2024 ) after 75 75 K pretraining updates and only 500 500 fine-tuning updates. Discrete tokens shaped by feature losses alone are therefore competitive with continuous representations while sampling at a fraction of the cost, which makes them a practical substrate for unified multimodal models. 2 Feature-loss tokenization In this section, we present FeaTok , which learns discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained visual features. We use this term to distinguish representations by their pretraining objective. Definition 1 . We define pretrained visual features as representations of encoders learned by self-supervision in feature space, including language–image contrastive learning ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) and self-distillation ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Siméoni et al., 2026 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . Encoders trained by pixel reconstruction ( He et al., 2022 ) are excluded. We next describe how FeaTok uses these features to train the tokenizer with feature losses (Fig. 2 ). 2.1 Learning discrete tokens with feature loss only Conventional discrete tokenizers ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ; Jia et al., 2025 ; Bachmann et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ; Yu et al., 2026 ) consist of an encoder E E , a quantizer Q Q , and a pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} . Given an image x x partitioned into N N patches, the encoder E E produces N N feature vectors, one per patch, which the quantizer Q Q maps to discrete tokens z 1 : N = Q ( E ( x ) ) z_{1:N}=Q(E(x)) . The pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} then reconstructs the image as x ^ = D pix ( z 1 : N ) \hat{x}=D_{\rm pix}(z_{1:N}) . Tokenizers are typically trained as an autoencoder with a pixel-level objective ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm pix} that combines pixel reconstruction losses ( ℓ 1 \ell_{1} , ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ), perceptual losses (LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , GRAM ( Lu et al., 2026a ) ), and adversarial losses ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) . Once the tokenizer is trained, an autoregressive model conditioned on class labels or text prompts c c learns the distribution p ϕ ( z 1 : N ∣ c ) p_{\phi}(z_{1:N}\mid c) of the resulting token sequences using the cross-entropy loss. Shaping discrete tokens with feature losses. FeaTok follows the autoencoder-style tokenizer design, but learns the discrete tokens by reconstructing features rather than pixels (see Fig. 2 ). Concretely, we add a feature decoder D feat D_{\rm feat} that maps the discrete tokens z 1 : N z_{1:N} to a prediction y ^ 1 : N = D feat ( z 1 : N ) \hat{y}_{1:N}=D_{\rm feat}(z_{1:N}) of a feature target y 1 : N y_{1:N} . We train the encoder, quantizer, and feature decoder to match this prediction to the target using a loss ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm feat} that combines ℓ 1 \ell_{1} , ℓ 2 \ell_{2} , and cosine distances. For the feature target, following the insights in Singh et al. (2026) , we use an average of features from multiple layers of the frozen vision encoder E ^ \hat{E} , y 1 : N ( x ) = | 𝒦 | − 1 ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 LN k ( E ^ ( k ) ( x ) 1 : N ) y_{1:N}(x)=|\mathcal{K}|^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\operatorname{LN}_{k}(\hat{E}^{(k)}(x)_{1:N}) , where 𝒦 \mathcal{K} contains four evenly spaced encoder layers and LayerNorm ( Ba et al., 2016 ) normalizes each layer’s features before averaging. This target is intended to combine visual detail from earlier layers with semantic information from later layers, balancing expressivity and generative learnability. While we retain the pixel decoder D pix D_{\rm pix} and its pixel-level loss ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm{pix}} during training, we stop the gradients at the decoder input. This preserves the ability to decode tokens back into images while preventing the pixel reconstruction losses from shaping the token distribution. Figure 2: FeaTok tokenizer and generation pipeline. Blue denotes the conventional discrete tokenizer and orange our contributions. Only feature losses shape the discrete tokens: ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm feat} trains D feat D_{\rm feat} to reconstruct the multi-layer target y y of the frozen encoder E ^ \hat{E} from both global and patch tokens, while ℒ pix \mathcal{L}_{\rm pix} trains only D pix D_{\rm pix} on detached patch tokens. The generator (not shown) models the global token from Q global Q_{\rm global} together with the patch tokens from Q patch Q_{\rm patch} . Leveraging global tokens. In addition to patch features, various vision encoders supply a global representation, e.g. , a CLS token in DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Siméoni et al., 2026 ) or a global pooling token in SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . Replacing pixel reconstruction with feature reconstruction losses naturally suggests discretizing this global feature along with patches. The benefit of doing so is that it allows us to define a hierarchical generative model that first generates the global token and then the patch tokens conditioned on it which simplifies the conditional distributions of the patch tokens by providing a global context. This global representation is generally ignored by discrete tokenizers trained using pixel-reconstruction losses, as the pixel reconstruction over patches does not provide direct supervision on the global feature discretization. Prior work follows a similar global-to-local strategy, using learned holistic tokens ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) , coarse-to-fine token sequences ( Bachmann et al., 2025 ) , or separately generated semantic codes ( Lavoie et al., 2025 ) . In our case, the global token directly discretizes the pretrained encoder’s global representation. Specifically, we use separate quantizers, Q global Q_{\rm global} and Q patch Q_{\rm patch} , for global and patch features, respectively. The feature decoder D feat D_{\rm feat} takes both global and patch tokens and reconstructs the combined target y = ( y global , y 1 : N ) y=(y_{\rm global},y_{1:N}) using the feature loss ℒ feat \mathcal{L}_{\rm{feat}} . This yields a discrete global token z global z_{\rm global} , which we model jointly with the patch tokens using the following factorization: p ϕ ( z global , z 1 : N ∣ c ) = p ϕ ( z global ∣ c ) ∏ i = 1 N p ϕ ( z i ∣ z global , z < i , c ) . p_{\phi}(z_{\rm global},z_{1:N}\mid c)=p_{\phi}(z_{\rm global}\mid c)\,\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{\phi}(z_{i}\mid z_{\rm global},z_{<i},c). (1) where c c denotes the class label or text prompt. During inference, the generator first samples the global token and then samples patch tokens conditioned on both global and external conditions. Combined training objective. We train the tokenizer and pixel decoder jointly using the feature and pixel losses described above. Following prior work on semantic preservation during tokenizer training ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Du et al., 2026 ) , we also include an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularizer ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\rm reg} between the last-layer features h h and h ^ \hat{h} of the trainable and frozen encoders. With z = ( z global , z 1 : N ) z=(z_{\rm global},z_{1:N}) , the complete objective is ℒ FeaTok = 𝔼 x [ ℒ feat ​ ( D feat ​ ( z ) , y ) + λ reg ​ ℒ reg ​ ( h , h ^ ) ⏟ trains encoder, quantizers, feature decoder + λ pix ℒ pix ( D pix ( sg ( z 1 : N ) ) , x ) ⏟ trains only the pixel decoder ] , \mathcal{L}_{\rm FeaTok{}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\rm feat}\!\left(D_{\rm feat}(z),y\right)+\lambda_{\rm reg}\mathcal{L}_{\rm reg}(h,\hat{h})}_{\text{trains encoder, quantizers, feature decoder}}+\underbrace{\lambda_{\rm pix}\mathcal{L}_{\rm pix}\!\left(D_{\rm pix}\!\left(\operatorname{\mathrm{sg}}(z_{1:N})\right),x\right)}_{\text{trains only the pixel decoder}}\right], (2) where the expectation is over training images x x . The weights λ reg \lambda_{\rm reg} and λ pix \lambda_{\rm pix} balance the loss terms, and sg \mathrm{sg} stops gradients at the pixel decoder input. Once the tokenizer is trained, we keep it fixed and train an autoregressive generator on its tokens using teacher forcing. We combine the cross-entropy loss for the global token with the average loss over patch tokens, weighted by λ global \lambda_{\rm global} and λ patch \lambda_{\rm patch} , respectively. These weights control the emphasis on global and patch prediction independently of the number of patches. 2.2 Controlled ablations across pretrained vision encoders \subfloat [Tokenizer targets.] \subfloat [Spatial dependence.] \subfloat [Global augmentation.] Figure 3: Tokenizer-target and generator-type ablations. (a) With patch-only generation, feature targets improve gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3. The DINOv3 pixel bar has a break to accommodate its gFID of 2.92 2.92 . (b) Spatial dependence between adjacent patch tokens versus patch-only gFID. The feature target raises the dependence and lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3. Both axes are log-scaled. (c) With the feature target fixed, global-augmented generation improves gFID for all four encoders, achieving better generation than pixel-target baselines. We verify FeaTok, feature-loss tokenization, against pixel-loss tokenization using four pretrained vision encoders: SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , and DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) . We compare the generation performance of a generative model trained on ImageNet-1k ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) images at × 256 256\!\times\!256 resolution using different tokenizers. Details of ablation setups are given in App. C . Additionally, App. C.2 shows that tokenizers built on MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) , whose features are learned by pixel reconstruction, generate poorly under every supervision. Feature targets work better than pixel-only or mixed feature–pixel targets. Feature supervision improves the generation over pixel supervision for three of the four encoders, as shown in Fig. 3 . With patch-only generation, replacing pixel targets with feature targets lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, while combining pixel and feature losses, i.e. , letting gradients from both decoders update the discrete tokens, gives intermediate results. Fig. 3 relates these gFID changes to the spatial dependence between adjacent discrete patch tokens. Full prompts are available in Tab. 17 . 4 Related work Pretrained representations for continuous generation. Continuous generators show that the pretraining objective of the features matters. RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) and RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) train diffusion models in the feature spaces of pretrained vision encoders, paired with learned image decoders, and RAE finds that MAE features ( He et al., 2022 ) reconstruct best but generate worse than DINOv2 features. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025b ) aligns intermediate SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ) features with pretrained representations, where MAE is the weakest of the tested targets, and DDT ( Wang et al., 2026 ) adopts this alignment. REG ( Wu et al., 2025 ) denoises a pretrained class token together with the image latents, VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns VAE latents with a pretrained vision encoder, and REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025 ) tunes the VAE and the diffusion model end to end with the REPA loss. Discrete tokenization with pretrained representations. VQ-VAE ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ) learns discrete image tokens through pixel reconstruction, and later tokenizers simplify the quantizer ( Yu et al., 2024a ; Mentzer et al., 2024 ) . Wang et al. (2024) train tokenizers to reconstruct the features from image understanding encoders, and in autoregressive generation all but the MAE teacher outperform pixel-trained VQGAN tokens. Recent tokenizers keep pixel reconstruction as the central objective and add pretrained encoder features through feature alignment ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , semantic regularization ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) , self-distillation ( Du et al., 2026 ) , or feature reconstruction from several encoder depths ( Jia et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) . TA-Tok ( Han et al., 2025 ) trains feature-reconstructed tokens for unified multimodal models, but decodes images through pixel-trained VQ tokens or latents. In FeaTok, only pretrained visual features (Def. 1 ) shape the tokens, which reconstruct a multi-layer target and include a quantized global token. 5 Conclusion We presented FeaTok, a discrete image tokenizer whose tokens are shaped only by feature reconstruction, while a pixel decoder trained on detached tokens renders them into images. We also discretize the encoder’s global representation and model it together with the patch tokens. Across four pretrained encoders, FeaTok generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses. FeaTok achieves the best gFDr6 among the evaluated discrete generators on ImageNet at × 256 256\!\times\!256 and × 512 512\!\times\!512 , outperforms continuous generators at a matched sampling cost, achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores, and transfers to text-to-image generation after pretraining and only 500 500 fine-tuning updates. We believe these results are a step toward effective discrete representations for unified multimodal modeling, and that the low sampling cost of FeaTok makes it attractive for scaling multimodal training.
